articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.1 Million Tourism Marketing Contract Went to a Firm With No Public Track Record
articles.dek: The TDC approved the deal in a 45-second vote. Six months later, the company still has no website, no portfolio, and no listed employees besides its owner—who previously worked in the county's tourism office.
brief: Escambia County's Tourist Development Council awarded a $2.1 million marketing contract to Gulf Horizon Media Group in December 2025, a company registered just three weeks before the bid submission deadline.
The firm's sole listed officer, Rachel Simmons, worked as a marketing coordinator in the county's tourism office until August 2025—four months before her company won the contract.
Six months into the contract, Gulf Horizon has no public website, no portfolio of previous work, and no employees listed on state or federal databases besides Simmons herself.
articles.body:
The conference room on the third floor of the Escambia County Central Office Complex seats maybe forty people. On the morning of December 12, 2025, seven of those seats were filled—five Tourist Development Council members, a county attorney, and a clerk. The agenda listed eleven items. Item 8B, a $2.1 million marketing services contract, took 45 seconds.

No discussion. No questions about the winning bidder. TDC Chair Marcus Webb read the item number, asked for a motion, got one, got a second, called for a vote. Five ayes. Next item.

That bidder was Gulf Horizon Media Group LLC. According to Florida Division of Corporations records, the company was registered on October 18, 2025—exactly 21 days before the November 8 bid deadline. Its registered agent and sole listed officer is Rachel Simmons, 34, of Pensacola.

Until August 2025, Simmons worked inside the Escambia County tourism office as a marketing coordinator. She reported to Tourism Director Patricia Haines, who sat in that December meeting as a non-voting advisor to the TDC.

Haines did not respond to three requests for comment over a two-week period. Simmons did not return calls to a number listed on her company's state filing. Webb, the TDC chair, said through a county spokesperson that board members "rely on staff recommendations for vendor qualifications" and declined further comment.

A Company That Doesn't Appear to Exist

Six months after winning the contract, Gulf Horizon Media Group has no website. A Google search returns only the Florida corporate filing and a brief mention in the December TDC meeting minutes.

The company has no LinkedIn page. No Facebook business profile. No portfolio of previous campaigns, client lists, or case studies available through any public channel The Flightline could locate.

A search of the Florida Department of State's annual report database shows Gulf Horizon has filed one document since its creation—the initial articles of organization. No annual report has been submitted, though one won't be required until 2026.

The company's registered address is a UPS Store mailbox on North Davis Highway. A visit to that location confirmed the box exists but staff declined to provide any information about the account holder.

According to the U.S. Small Business Administration's database of federal contractors, Gulf Horizon has no federal contract history. The company does not appear in the System for Award Management, the federal government's contractor registration database.

Florida's re-employment assistance records—which track quarterly wage reports filed by employers—show no employees reported by a company matching Gulf Horizon's federal employer identification number as of March 2026, according to a public records request filed with the Florida Department of Economic Opportunity. The department noted this could indicate the company uses only independent contractors or has not yet filed its first quarterly report.

The Bid Process

Escambia County issued Request for Proposals 26-017, "Destination Marketing Services," on October 15, 2025. The 47-page document sought a vendor to handle advertising, social media management, content creation, and media buying for Visit Pensacola, the county's tourism marketing arm.

The RFP required bidders to submit examples of previous destination marketing campaigns, a list of current clients, staff qualifications, and a detailed work plan. It set the contract term at three years with two optional one-year extensions, for a potential total value of $3.5 million.

Three companies submitted bids by the November 8 deadline: Gulf Horizon Media Group, Coastal Creative Partners of Destin, and Spark Tourism Marketing of Atlanta.

The Flightline obtained scoring sheets through a public records request. A three-person evaluation committee—all county employees—ranked the proposals on a 100-point scale covering experience, approach, qualifications, and cost.

Gulf Horizon received an average score of 87. Coastal Creative received 84. Spark Tourism received 79.

The scoring sheets included brief comments. Under "experience," one evaluator wrote that Gulf Horizon's proposal "demonstrates strong understanding of Pensacola market." Another noted "creative approach to targeting drive markets."

The proposal itself, obtained through the same records request, is 34 pages. It includes market analysis data, campaign concepts, and budget breakdowns. What it does not include is any evidence of previous work.

The "past performance" section—which the RFP designated as worth 25 of 100 points—contains two paragraphs. The first describes Simmons' seven years of marketing experience "in the Florida Gulf Coast tourism sector." The second states that Gulf Horizon "brings fresh perspective unconstrained by legacy client relationships."

No client names. No campaign examples. No performance metrics.

Asked how Gulf Horizon scored 22 of 25 possible points in that category, county purchasing director Allison McCarty said the evaluation committee's deliberations are confidential. "Evaluators are instructed to score based on the totality of information submitted," she said. "Individual scoring rationale is not documented beyond committee discussion."

The Simmons Connection

Rachel Simmons joined Escambia County's tourism office in July 2022 as a marketing coordinator, according to county human resources records obtained through a public records request. Her starting salary was $52,000.

Her job duties included coordinating advertising placements, managing vendor relationships, and assisting with campaign development. She reported to Tourism Director Patricia Haines.

Simmons resigned effective August 18, 2025, according to her personnel file. The file contains no exit interview, no stated reason for departure, and no documentation of any disputes or disciplinary issues.

Sixty-one days later, Gulf Horizon Media Group was registered with the state.

Florida Statute 112.313, the state's ethics law, prohibits former public employees from representing private clients before their former agency for two years after leaving public employment. However, the statute includes an exemption for competitively bid contracts.

"If a contract is awarded through a competitive process, the two-year prohibition does not apply," said Steven Kahn, an attorney with the Florida Commission on Ethics who spoke generally about the statute and not about this specific case. "The theory is that competitive bidding provides sufficient safeguard against favoritism."

The law does not prohibit former employees from bidding on contracts with their former agencies. It also does not require bidders to disclose previous employment relationships with the contracting entity.

Gulf Horizon's proposal makes no mention of Simmons' county employment history.

What the Contract Requires

The three-year contract, signed December 19, 2025, obligates Gulf Horizon to deliver a specific list of services: development of an annual marketing plan, creation of advertising content for television, radio, digital, and print platforms, management of Visit Pensacola's social media accounts, and monthly performance reports.

The county agreed to pay $58,333 per month—$700,000 annually—with additional funds available for approved media buys.

According to invoices obtained through public records, Gulf Horizon has billed the county $350,000 through May 2026. The invoices list work performed in categories matching the contract's scope but provide no granular detail—no breakdowns of hours worked, no identification of specific deliverables, no itemization of subcontractor costs.

Visit Pensacola's social media accounts show regular posting activity since January, including beach photography, event promotions, and video content featuring local restaurants and attractions. The posts do not credit a creator.

The tourism office's website lists a summer advertising campaign launching this month. A county spokesperson confirmed Gulf Horizon produced the campaign materials but declined to make samples available before the public launch.

TDC Members Say They Trusted the Process

The Tourist Development Council operates as an advisory body to the Escambia County Commission. Its five members include three hospitality industry representatives, one county commissioner, and one at-large appointee. All serve without compensation.

Member Janet Prichard, who owns a vacation rental management company on Pensacola Beach, voted to approve the Gulf Horizon contract. In an interview, she said she had not researched the company before the vote.

"We get staff recommendations," Prichard said. "I've been on this board four years. I don't recall ever voting against a staff recommendation on a vendor. That's not really our role."

Asked whether she was aware Simmons had worked for the tourism office, Prichard said she was not. "I don't know who that is," she said. "I assume if there was a conflict, staff would have flagged it."

TDC member Robert Chen, general manager of the Hilton Pensacola Beach, also voted yes. He did not respond to interview requests.

The lone county commissioner on the TDC, District 4 representative Douglas Underwood, said through a spokesperson that he "supports the competitive procurement process" and has "full confidence in county staff's vendor review procedures."

What Remains Unknown

Several basic questions about Gulf Horizon Media Group remain unanswered after two months of reporting:

Does the company have employees? Simmons is the only name associated with the firm in any public record. The proposal submitted to the county references a "team" but names no individuals besides Simmons.

Who performs the work? The company may use subcontractors, but the contract requires county approval for subcontractors receiving more than $25,000. No such approvals appear in TDC records through May 2026.

Has Simmons performed any work herself? Without knowing the company's structure, it's impossible to determine who creates the content appearing on Visit Pensacola's platforms.

What previous experience justified the winning score? The proposal contained no verifiable evidence of past work. Simmons' county employment history is not mentioned in any procurement document.

Simmons did not respond to a detailed list of questions sent to the email address on Gulf Horizon's state filing, to the phone number on the same filing, or to a letter sent to the registered business address.

Tourism Director Haines did not respond to the same list of questions sent via email and certified mail to her county office.

County Administrator Wes Moreno declined an interview request but provided a written statement: "Escambia County follows all applicable procurement laws and regulations. The marketing services contract was awarded through a competitive, publicly advertised process open to all qualified bidders."

The Broader Pattern

Tourism marketing contracts have drawn scrutiny in Florida before. In 2019, the state's tourism marketing agency, Visit Florida, faced legislative criticism over contracts with vendors that had personal connections to agency leadership. The resulting controversy contributed to years of funding battles and calls for agency dissolution.

At the local level, tourist development councils across Florida operate with minimal oversight. Funded by a dedicated "bed tax" on hotel stays rather than general tax revenue, they exist in a bureaucratic middle ground—public bodies spending public money but often without the scrutiny applied to other government functions.

Escambia County's bed tax generated $18.2 million in fiscal year 2025, according to county budget documents. The TDC directs spending of approximately $6 million of that total, with the remainder going to beach maintenance, sports facilities, and cultural attractions.

The $700,000 annual marketing contract represents roughly 12 percent of the TDC's discretionary budget.

"Tourist development councils are where transparency goes to die," said Maria Santos, a professor of public administration at Florida State University who studies local government accountability. "You have industry insiders advising on contracts that benefit their industry, staff who rotate between public and private roles, and boards that meet during business hours when the public isn't watching. It's a structural problem, not just a personnel problem."

The TDC's next meeting is scheduled for July 10, 2026, at 9 a.m. in the Escambia County Central Office Complex. Gulf Horizon's six-month performance review is on the agenda.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The 12-Story Shadow Over Pensacola Beach
articles.dek: A proposed resort tower would be the tallest structure on the island. Neighbors say it violates the county's own height limits. The developer says those limits don't apply. Both cite the same 1984 land use plan.
brief: A Miami-based developer has proposed a 12-story, 156-foot resort tower for a 2.3-acre parcel on Via de Luna, which would become the tallest structure on Pensacola Beach

Opponents argue the project violates the Santa Rosa Island Authority's 75-foot height limit, while the developer claims the parcel's 'high-density resort' designation exempts it under the 1984 land use plan
The dispute hinges on conflicting interpretations of a 40-year-old document that governs development on the barrier island
articles.body:
The rendering shows a glass tower catching the afternoon sun, its shadow stretching east across the sand toward the quieter residential stretch of Pensacola Beach. Twelve stories. One hundred fifty-six feet. Taller than anything else on the island by a margin of five floors.

Coastal Horizon Development LLC, a Miami-based firm, submitted the proposal to the Santa Rosa Island Authority in April. The company wants to build a 187-room resort with ground-floor retail, a rooftop restaurant, and a parking structure on 2.3 acres along Via de Luna Drive, just west of the Portofino towers.

Within weeks, the SRIA received 340 written objections from leaseholders. Their argument is simple: the island has a 75-foot height limit. The tower would exceed it by 81 feet.

The developer's argument is also simple: that limit doesn't apply here.

Both sides cite the same document — the 1984 Santa Rosa Island Land Use Plan — as proof.

What the plan actually says

The 1984 plan divided Pensacola Beach into zones with different density allowances and building restrictions. Most of the island falls under designations that cap structures at 75 feet or less. The Portofino towers, completed in 2005 and 2007, reached their 17-story heights through a negotiated development agreement that predated stricter enforcement.

The Coastal Horizon parcel sits in an area the 1984 plan designated as 'High-Density Resort Commercial.' According to the document, this zone was intended for 'major resort facilities' that would serve as economic anchors for the island.

Here's where the interpretations diverge.

The plan's Section 4.3.2 establishes the 75-foot limit for 'all structures on Santa Rosa Island.' But Section 6.1.4, which governs the High-Density Resort Commercial zone, states that 'building heights shall be determined through site plan review based on compatibility with adjacent uses and environmental impact considerations.'

Coastal Horizon's attorney, Rebecca Vance of the Tallahassee firm Carlton Fields, argues this language creates an exception. 'The drafters clearly intended for major resort projects to undergo individualized review rather than be subject to a blanket cap,' Vance wrote in an April 28 letter to the SRIA.

Opponents read it differently. 'Section 4.3.2 says all structures,' said Tom Henning, a Via de Luna leaseholder who has organized opposition to the project. 'There's no asterisk. There's no exception clause. If they wanted to exempt certain zones, they would have written that.'

The SRIA's dilemma

The Santa Rosa Island Authority, a five-member board appointed by Escambia County, has scheduled a preliminary hearing on the project for July 15. But the board faces a problem that extends beyond this single development.

In the 42 years since the land use plan was adopted, the SRIA has never formally resolved the apparent conflict between Sections 4.3.2 and 6.1.4. The Portofino towers were approved through a process that involved the county commission directly. No other developer has tested the High-Density Resort Commercial provision since.

'We're essentially being asked to interpret a document that two reasonable people can read two different ways,' said SRIA board member Janet Kirkland at the board's June 3 meeting. 'And whatever we decide is going to set precedent.'

The board has requested a formal opinion from the Escambia County Attorney's office. That opinion is expected before the July 15 hearing but has not been made public.

The environmental question

Height limits on barrier islands aren't arbitrary aesthetic preferences. They serve specific purposes: reducing wind load during hurricanes, limiting shadow impact on dune vegetation, and preserving sight lines that help with emergency evacuation.

Pensacola Beach sits on a barrier island that has been overwashed by storm surge three times since 2004 — during Hurricanes Ivan, Dennis, and Sally. The island's emergency evacuation route, the Bob Sikes Bridge, can handle approximately 2,400 vehicles per hour under optimal conditions. Current peak-season population already strains that capacity.

Coastal Horizon's proposal includes an environmental impact assessment conducted by Atkins North America. The assessment concludes the tower's shadow would not significantly affect dune vegetation east of the site due to the angle of afternoon sun. It also notes the building would be designed to current Florida Building Code hurricane standards, which have been strengthened substantially since Portofino was built.

Critics point out that the assessment was commissioned by the developer. 'Of course their consultant found what they wanted to find,' Henning said. 'We're asking for an independent review.'

What happens next

The July 15 hearing will not result in a final decision. It's classified as a 'preliminary site plan review,' which means the board will determine whether the project can proceed to full review or must be denied on threshold grounds — including the height question.

If the SRIA determines the 75-foot limit applies, Coastal Horizon would need to either redesign the project or seek a variance from the county commission. If the board accepts the developer's interpretation, opponents have indicated they will file suit.

'This isn't about one building,' said Maria Santos, who leases a home on Ariola Drive east of the proposed site. 'It's about what Pensacola Beach becomes. If they can build 12 stories, someone else can build 15. Where does it stop?'

Coastal Horizon declined to make representatives available for an interview. In a written statement, the company said it 'looks forward to working with the SRIA and the community to develop a world-class resort that will benefit the island's economy while respecting its character.'

The 1984 plan was written when Pensacola Beach's year-round population was under 1,000. It's now closer to 3,500, with seasonal peaks many times that. The document's authors could not have anticipated a proposal like this one. But they're the ones whose words will decide it.

The SRIA meets at 5 p.m. on July 15 at the beach's visitor center. Public comment will be accepted.

articles.label: Feature
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Brings 200,000 Visitors and a Workforce Crisis
articles.dek: Hotels are overbooked. Restaurants are understaffed. And the seasonal workers who used to fill the gap aren't coming back. How Pensacola's biggest tourism week exposes a year-round labor problem.
brief: An estimated 200,000 visitors descended on Pensacola for Blue Angels Homecoming Week, but service industry employers report operating at 60-70% staffing levels
Local hotels turned away thousands of reservation requests while struggling to maintain housekeeping and front desk coverage
Business owners and workforce experts point to housing costs, wage competition, and post-pandemic migration as factors driving a structural labor shortage
articles.body:
At 6:47 a.m. on Thursday, Maria Santos unlocked the kitchen door at The Grand Marlin on Pensacola Beach and started prepping for what she knew would be the longest week of the year. By 7:15, she was on the phone with her manager. Two line cooks had called out. A third simply didn't answer.

"We do this every Homecoming," Santos said, pulling a case of shrimp from the walk-in cooler. "Run around trying to cover shifts. Beg people to stay late. It used to be we'd have seasonal kids lined up looking for work. Now? Nothing."

Outside, the first practice runs of F/A-18 Super Hornets carved white lines across a cloudless sky. By noon, traffic on Pensacola Beach Boulevard would back up past the Bob Sikes Bridge. By dinner, every restaurant on the island would have a two-hour wait and half the staff they needed to handle it.

Blue Angels Homecoming Week remains Pensacola's premier tourism event. Visit Pensacola estimates this year's crowds at 200,000 visitors over seven days, generating an economic impact north of $50 million. Hotel occupancy across Escambia and Santa Rosa counties hit 94% on show weekend. Short-term rental bookings on Pensacola Beach and Perdido Key approached sellout status weeks in advance.

But the businesses tasked with serving those visitors are operating in crisis mode. And the crisis didn't start this week.

The Numbers Don't Add Up

Escambia County's unemployment rate sat at 3.1% in May 2026, according to Florida Department of Economic Opportunity data. That's below the state average and well below the threshold economists consider "full employment." On paper, it looks like a success story.

On the ground, it looks like desperation.

"I have 47 rooms and enough housekeeping staff to turn maybe 30 of them in a day," said Robert Chen, general manager of the Holiday Inn Resort on Pensacola Beach. "We're paying $18 an hour plus tips for housekeepers. Five years ago that was $11. And I still can't fill the positions."

Chen said he turned away more than 400 reservation requests for Homecoming Week. Not because he lacked rooms. Because he lacked people to clean them.

The pattern repeats across the hospitality sector. A survey conducted by the Greater Pensacola Chamber in April found that 73% of local restaurants, hotels, and tourism-dependent businesses reported operating below optimal staffing levels. More than half said they had reduced hours or services due to labor shortages in the past year.

"This isn't a Homecoming problem," said Todd Thomson, the Chamber's vice president for economic development. "This is a year-round structural issue that Homecoming just makes impossible to ignore."

Where Did the Workers Go?

The simple answer: everywhere else.

The complicated answer involves housing, wages, demographics, and the long tail of a pandemic that reshuffled the American workforce in ways still playing out.

Start with housing. The median rent for a one-bedroom apartment in Pensacola proper rose to $1,340 per month in early 2026, according to Zillow data. That's up 47% from 2019. On Pensacola Beach, where many hospitality workers once lived in older apartment complexes and duplexes, median rents now exceed $2,100.

"A dishwasher making $14 an hour cannot afford to live within 30 minutes of the beach," said Dr. Angela Morrison, a labor economist at the University of West Florida. "So they work somewhere else. Or they leave entirely."

Morrison's research tracks migration patterns in Northwest Florida's service sector. She found that Escambia County lost approximately 2,400 hospitality workers between 2020 and 2025 who relocated to lower-cost markets in Alabama, Mississippi, and Georgia. Many were Hispanic workers who had formed the backbone of the region's housekeeping and kitchen staffs for decades.

"The pandemic broke a lot of those networks," Morrison said. "Workers went home to family. They found other jobs. They didn't come back. And the pipeline that used to bring new workers here dried up."

Immigration policy changes under successive administrations have also reduced the flow of J-1 visa workers who traditionally filled summer positions at beach resorts. The Holiday Inn's Chen said he used to hire 15 to 20 international students each summer. This year, he got three.

The Wage Competition Problem

Meanwhile, workers who do remain in the area have options they didn't have a decade ago.

Amazon's fulfillment center in Theodore, Alabama—45 minutes from downtown Pensacola—starts warehouse workers at $19 an hour with benefits and predictable schedules. The Navy Federal Credit Union campus in Beulah employs more than 10,000 people, many in entry-level positions paying $17 to $22 an hour with air conditioning and federal holidays off.

"I worked restaurants for eight years," said DeAndre Williams, 29, who now works in Navy Federal's call center. "Nights, weekends, doubles during tourist season. I make more money now sitting at a desk, and I'm home for dinner every night. Why would I go back?"

The calculus is straightforward. Hospitality work offers irregular hours, physical strain, and wages that haven't kept pace with alternatives. For a generation that watched their parents burn out in service jobs, the calculation increasingly favors exit.

Businesses Adapt—or Don't

Some Pensacola businesses have responded aggressively. Flounder's Chowder House on Pensacola Beach raised its minimum wage to $16 an hour and added retention bonuses for workers who stay through peak season. The Fish House downtown invested in automated ordering kiosks to reduce front-of-house staffing needs.

Others have simply cut back.

Three restaurants on Pensacola Beach operated on reduced schedules during Homecoming Week, closing for lunch to preserve staff for dinner service. At least two downtown hotels limited room service and concierge hours. One popular brunch spot on Palafox Street closed entirely for the weekend, citing "staffing challenges."

"I'd rather disappoint people by being closed than disappoint them with terrible service," said the restaurant's owner, who asked not to be named because she feared backlash from tourism boosters. "We just can't do it right with the people we have."

The Tourism Paradox

Visit Pensacola's marketing budget has grown 40% since 2019, part of a concerted effort to position the region as a year-round destination rather than a summer-only beach town. The campaign has worked. Visitor numbers are up. Hotel tax revenues have climbed. The Blue Angels brand remains one of the most powerful tourism draws in the Southeast.

But the infrastructure to support that growth hasn't kept pace.

"We've gotten very good at bringing people here," said Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes Pensacola Beach. "We haven't solved how to serve them once they arrive."

Bergosh said the county is exploring workforce housing initiatives, including a proposed development near the Pensacola Beach toll plaza that would offer below-market-rate units for hospitality workers. The project faces opposition from residents concerned about density and traffic.

"Nobody wants workforce housing in their backyard," Bergosh said. "But everybody wants their hotel room cleaned and their food served. Something has to give."

Back at The Grand Marlin

By Friday evening, Maria Santos had worked 14 hours. The kitchen was down to five cooks handling a dining room designed for eight. Ticket times stretched past 45 minutes. A table of four sent back their redfish. Twice.

Santos didn't complain. She's been doing this for 22 years, since before the beach rebuilt after Hurricane Ivan, before the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, before COVID emptied the restaurants and reshuffled everything.

"Every year they say it'll get better," she said, plating a blackened grouper with mechanical precision. "Every year it gets harder."

Outside, the Blue Angels made their final pass of the day, six jets in tight formation trailing smoke against an orange sunset. The crowd on the deck cheered. Cameras flashed. Somewhere in the distance, a car horn honked in the endless traffic.

Santos didn't look up. She had orders to fill.
